ACT I | Card 03 — Neuroscience
What's Actually Happening in the Social Brain
The Social Brain Circuit
At its core is the Superior Temporal Sulcus (STS), which processes the direction of other people's gaze. Connected to the Temporoparietal Junction (TPJ) and Prefrontal Cortex, this triadic network forms the foundation of all shared attention.
In ASD profiles, STS activity is reduced and less synchronized with the TPJ — the circuit that says "they are looking at something, therefore I should look too" is underconnected — not broken.
Wiring Can Be Strengthened
This is a wiring difference, not a behavior choice. And critically — wiring can be strengthened. Every time your child successfully follows your gaze, a neural pathway is reinforced.
Every bubble activity, every shared book, every musical turn-taking game is literal circuit-building. The social brain circuit learns to fire through deliberate, joyful, structured practice.

"This is not attention. This is not stubbornness. This is the social brain circuit learning to fire — and you are the activating agent."
Frontiers in Integrative Neuroscience (2020) | DOI:10.3389/fnint.2020.556660 | Charman, T. (2003) | DOI:10.1098/rstb.2002.1199

ACT II — THE KNOWLEDGE TRANSFER | Card 06
Joint Attention Building
Parent-friendly alias: "Teaching Your Child to Look Together"

Definition: Joint attention is the shared focus of two people on a single object or event — achieved through coordinated gaze, pointing, showing, or directing another person's attention. It has two components:

• Responding to Joint Attention (RJA): Following your gaze or point to see what you're looking at
• Initiating Joint Attention (IJA): Directing your attention — pointing to show you something, bringing you an object to share, or looking back and forth between you and something interesting

This is not eye contact. This is not compliance. This is the beginning of shared experience — the foundation of all human communication, language, and connection.

ACT II | Card 07 — Disciplines
Five Disciplines. One Child. One Foundational Skill.
🗣️ Speech-Language Pathology (PRIMARY LEAD)
SLPs deploy joint attention as the prerequisite to ALL language intervention. A child cannot learn a word unless both child and adult are attending to the same referent. Every vocabulary session begins with establishing joint attention. Every communication target depends on it.
🖐️ Occupational Therapy
OTs address sensory and motor barriers that prevent joint attention — hypersensitivity that makes eye contact aversive, proprioceptive seeking that pulls attention away from social partners, low arousal that reduces social engagement. OT creates the regulatory platform for joint attention to emerge.
🎯 ABA / BCBA
BCBAs structure joint attention trials using Pivotal Response Training (PRT) and Natural Environment Teaching (NET) — making joint attention a pivotal skill that cascades to all other developmental domains. ABA data systems track RJA and IJA frequency across sessions.
📚 Special Education
SpEd specialists embed joint attention goals across classroom activities — circle time, shared reading, show-and-tell, group activities. They train teachers and aides in positioning and response strategies that create joint attention opportunities throughout the school day.
🧠 NeuroDevelopmental Pediatrics / CRO
NeuroDev physicians assess joint attention as a core diagnostic marker (ADOS-2, M-CHAT). They prescribe intervention intensity based on RJA/IJA baseline scores and track progress against developmental norms.

"This technique crosses therapy boundaries because the brain doesn't organize by therapy type. Joint attention is everyone's responsibility — and every professional's entry point."
📞9100 181 181 | Multi-disciplinary assessment available at 70+ Pinnacle centers
ACT II | Card 08 — Targets
Precision Targeting: What Joint Attention Actually Builds
🎯 Primary Targets
Responding to Joint Attention (RJA) + Initiating Joint Attention (IJA). Child follows adult's gaze and point. Child initiates: points to show, brings items, gaze-alternates. Observable: triadic gaze shifts.
🎯 Secondary Targets
Language Acquisition | Social Referencing | Imitation | Turn-Taking. Word learning accelerates when child follows adult's attention to the named object. The "my turn / your turn" social rhythm.
🎯 Tertiary Targets
Theory of Mind | Pretend Play | Academic Readiness | Friendship Formation. Shared pretend, following teacher's attention in classroom, social bonding that creates reciprocal friendships.
Observable Behavior Indicators — When Joint Attention Is Developing:
  • ✅ Child looks where you point (not at your finger)
  • ✅ Child looks at you, then at toy, then back at you
  • ✅ Child brings you something just to show you (not to get help)
  • ✅ Child points at airplanes/dogs/interesting things to share them
  • ✅ Child checks your face when uncertain
PMC10955541 | Charman (2003) DOI:10.1098/rstb.2002.1199 | Kasari et al. (2006)
ACT II | Card 09 — Material 01
Material 01: Bubble Wands and Bubble Machines 🫧
Joint Attention Mechanism
Attention Capture + Adult-as-Source
Bubbles come from YOU. The child must look toward you to see more. Pause with the wand near your face — the child looks at you, then at the bubble, then back. That gaze shift IS joint attention.
Why It Works
The child cannot access the motivating stimulus (bubbles) without orienting toward you. You become the necessary social gateway to something wonderful. Every pause is a practice opportunity.
DIY Option — ₹0
2 tbsp dish soap + 1 tbsp glycerin + 1 cup water | Wire bent into a loop for the wand. Blow near your face. Pause. Wait for gaze.
Buy
Bubble wands ₹50–500 | Battery machines ₹300–800
🔗 [Search Amazon.in: bubble wand kids India]
Safety Notes
  • Non-toxic solution only — children may taste it
  • Supervise closely around slippery floors
  • Wipe up spills immediately to prevent falls

Starter Recommendation: This is the #1 entry material for most children. Start here before any other material in the kit.
ACT II | Card 09 — Material 02
Material 02: Cause-and-Effect Toys 🤖
Joint Attention Mechanism
Look-to-Request
Only YOU can make the toy work. Toy does something exciting → stops → child looks at YOU to request more. That look-to-request is RJA in action. You are the controller. The child must find you to continue the experience.
Why It Works
The toy's activation becomes contingent on social orientation. The child learns: "Looking at people makes interesting things happen." This is the neural pathway we are building.
DIY Option — ₹0
Any container with a lid you control, any toy you operate — the principle matters more than the product. Your hand is the cause. The effect is the interesting event.
Buy
Wind-up toys ₹200–600 | Pop-up toys ₹300–900
🔗 [Search Amazon.in: wind up cause effect toy toddler]
Canon Match: Dyomnizy Educational Memory Game ₹519
Safety Notes
  • Check for small parts — choking hazard for under 3
  • Supervise button batteries closely
  • Inspect for sharp edges before use
ACT II | Card 09 — Material 03
Material 03: Interactive Books with Flaps and Textures 📖
Joint Attention Mechanism
Point-and-Find
Lift-the-flap books create natural "where is it?" moments. Parent points → child follows the point → shared delight at the reveal. Every flap is a triadic attention opportunity built naturally into a beloved routine.
Why It Works
Books scaffold joint attention because the content is predictable (child learns what's coming) yet surprising (the reveal). This balance of anticipation and discovery is neurologically optimal for joint attention learning.
DIY Option — ₹0
Make your own flap book with cardstock and drawings or printed photos. Draw or paste a picture. Fold paper over it as a flap. "What's under here?" — lift only when child looks at your pointing finger's target.
Buy
Lift-the-flap board books ₹250–800
🔗 [Search Amazon.in: lift flap board book toddler]
Safety Notes
  • Board book format for children under 3 — prevents tearing
  • Supervise paper books to prevent ingestion
  • Laminate DIY versions for durability

Pro Tip: Family photo flap books (familiar faces under the flaps) produce the highest motivation and the most consistent joint attention responses.
ACT II | Card 09 — Material 04
Material 04: Light-Up and Glow Toys 💡
Joint Attention Mechanism
Visual Salience + Directed Gaze
Light naturally draws gaze. Hold a light-up toy near your face in a dim room — the child looks toward the light source, toward YOU. Use light wands as enhanced pointing tools that are easier to follow than bare fingers — especially for children with motor vision challenges.
Why It Works
The visual system is wired to orient toward luminance changes. By placing the light-source near your face, you harness this primitive orienting reflex to deliver the child's gaze to the social target — YOU.
DIY Option — ₹0
Household flashlight used as pointing tool. Shine on wall objects. "Look! On the door!" Child follows beam = enhanced RJA practice. Dim the room slightly for maximum visual salience.
Buy
Light-up wands ₹100–400 | Star projectors ₹500–1,200
🔗 [Search Amazon.in: light up glow wand kids]
Canon Match: COOLCOLD Laser Light pointer ₹579
Safety Notes
  • NEVER shine directly in eyes — serious injury risk
  • Soft, diffused light preferred over sharp beams
  • Laser pointers: indirect use on walls/floors only
  • Check battery compartment is secure
ACT II | Card 09 — Material 05
Material 05: Pointing Finger Puppets and Pointing Wands 👆
Joint Attention Mechanism
Enhanced Gesture Salience
When a fuzzy puppet points, children follow it more reliably than bare fingers. "Mr. Pointer sees something! What is he looking at?" The pointing gesture is externalized into something concrete, named, and followable — making RJA more accessible for children who struggle with abstract finger-following.
Why It Works
Children with ASD often look at the pointing finger rather than where it points. A puppet with a named character transforms the gesture into a social invitation — "where is Mr. Pointer looking?" — which scaffolds the gaze-shift naturally.
DIY Option — ₹10–30
Decorate a pencil with googly eyes + cardboard pointing finger with index finger extended. Name it. "Mr. Pointer sees something on the shelf!" Give the puppet a consistent name and personality.
Buy
Character wands ₹100–500 | Finger puppets ₹50–300
🔗 [Search Amazon.in: pointing finger puppet wand kids]
Safety Notes
  • No sharp ends — check wand tips
  • Supervise to prevent throwing
  • Small finger puppets: choking risk under age 3

Tip: Lightly tap the target object with the puppet to add a movement cue — this is especially helpful for children who look at the pointer rather than the target.
ACT II | Card 09 — Material 06
Material 06: Musical Instruments with Social Turn-Taking 🥁
Joint Attention Mechanism
Watch-to-Take-Turns
Each person has an instrument. The child must WATCH you to know when their turn begins. Parent stops playing and looks at child expectantly — child watches and responds. Music makes social watching feel natural and joyful rather than demanded. The rhythm of turn-taking becomes the scaffold for joint attention.
Why It Works
Music creates a temporal structure that makes "wait and watch" feel like play rather than instruction. The predictable beat helps the child anticipate — and anticipation drives social gaze toward the partner who controls the next event.
DIY Option — ₹0
Two spoons as percussion | Clapping games | Rice in a sealed bottle as shaker | Any rhythmic body movement. The instrument is secondary to the turn-taking structure.
Buy
Small drums ₹200–600 | Shakers/maracas ₹100–400
🔗 [Search Amazon.in: kids drum shaker musical instrument set]
Safety Notes
  • Child-safe instruments only
  • No small detachable parts
  • Volume check for auditorily sensitive children
  • Avoid sharp instrument edges
ACT II | Card 09 — Material 07
Material 07: Surprise Boxes and Mystery Bags 🎁
Joint Attention Mechanism
Anticipatory Attention + Social Referencing
"What's inside?" The child is compelled to look at the container AND at you — the person controlling the reveal. Shared anticipation + shared discovery = triadic joint attention at its richest. The mystery box combines RJA (looking toward you to understand the situation) with social referencing (checking your face for emotional information).
Why It Works
Uncertainty is a powerful driver of social gaze. When children don't know what's coming, they naturally look to the knowledgeable adult — YOU — for information. The mystery box harnesses this developmental instinct.
DIY Option — ₹0
Any container with a lid + household objects inside. Shake dramatically. "What is that sound?!" Reveal together. A repurposed food tin or shoebox works perfectly — the child's favorite toy hidden inside produces the highest motivation.
Buy
Decorative boxes ₹50–400 | Fabric drawstring bags ₹100–300
🔗 [Search Amazon.in: mystery box surprise bag kids activity]
Safety Notes
  • No choking hazards inside — check every item
  • Supervise bag play — strangulation risk with drawstrings
  • Ensure box edges are smooth and safe
ACT II | Card 09 — Material 08
Material 08: Social Games — Peekaboo Props and Chase Items 🙈
Joint Attention Mechanism
Person-Focused Attention
Peekaboo and chase make YOU the most interesting thing to watch — not a toy, not a screen, YOU. The child's entire attention is on the social partner. Joy + person-focus = the most fundamental joint attention training possible. These games require no objects at all — the relationship IS the material.
Why It Works
Person-focused games bypass the need for triadic attention entirely and build the foundation of social interest. Before a child can share attention about objects, they must find people interesting. Peekaboo makes you fascinating.
DIY Option — ₹0
Scarf from any wardrobe for peekaboo | Your own body for chase | Hiding behind furniture | Hands over face. The most powerful joint attention material in existence costs nothing.
Buy
Peekaboo scarves ₹50–300 | Tickle toys ₹50–200
🔗 [Search Amazon.in: peekaboo scarf baby toddler game]
Safety Notes
  • Choose scarves without strangulation risk — lightweight, open-weave
  • Clear space before chase games — remove obstacles
  • Ensure child can easily remove scarf from face

Note: If your child engages with peekaboo but not other materials, start here and build toward object-directed joint attention gradually.
ACT II | Card 09 — Material 09
Material 09: Photo Books of Familiar People and Places 📷
Joint Attention Mechanism
High-Motivation Shared Attention
Photos of Mama, Papa, Dadi, the dog — content the child actually cares about. "Look! There's Dadi!" The child wants to see familiar faces → follows your point → gaze alternation between photo and you. Personally relevant content maximizes motivation, making joint attention practice feel natural rather than therapeutic.
Why It Works
Familiar faces activate the strongest social brain responses. The child already has emotional investment in these images — you simply need to position yourself as the gateway to seeing them, creating irresistible reasons to look toward you.
DIY Option — ₹50–150
Print 10 family photos at local shop (₹5 each). Laminate with tape. Punch holes. Tie with ribbon. Done. This is the highest-impact DIY option on the entire list — and the most personally relevant for your child.
Buy
Photo albums ₹200–500 | Digital on tablet ₹0
🔗 [Search Amazon.in: photo album small pocket prints]
Safety Notes
  • Laminate printed pages for durability with young children
  • Tape down any loose lamination edges
  • Tablet screens: limit exposure for very young children

Starter Kit Recommendation: Begin with bubbles + 1 lift-the-flap book + family photo prints + a scarf. Total: ₹150–500. All high-impact, zero-risk entry materials.

ACT II | Card 10 — DIY & Secondary Materials
Every Material Has a ₹0 Version
Secondary Materials
  • Sensory bins with hidden objects (finding game = joint attention)
  • Windmills / pinwheels (visual tracking + "look at that!")
  • Kaleidoscopes (visual fascination + "look what I found!")

💡DIY Light Pointer: Household torch. Shine on wall objects. "Look! On the door!" Child follows beam = enhanced RJA practice.
🎁DIY Mystery Box: Any food container with lid. Hide child's favorite toy inside. Shake dramatically. "What is that sound?!" Reveal together.
👆DIY Pointer Puppet: Pencil + googly eyes + cardboard cut-out hand with index finger extended. Name it. "Mr. Pointer sees something!"

ACT II | Card 11 — Safety
Safety First: What Every Parent Must Know
Before beginning any joint attention activities at home, review these safety guidelines carefully. When in doubt, call 9100 181 181 — our team speaks 16+ languages and is available 24x7.
✅ Safe to Do at Home
All 9 materials at home dosage (10–20 min sessions) | Bubble play with non-toxic solution | Light-up toys at safe distances (never direct in eyes) | Peekaboo and chase in safe spaces | DIY photo books and pointing games | Musical turn-taking with child-safe instruments | Surprise boxes with age-appropriate contents
⚠️ Modify with Caution
Children with significant eye contact aversion — do NOT force. Create inviting contexts, never demand looking | Children who bolt during chase — enclosed, safe spaces only | Laser pointer alternatives — indirect on walls/floors only, never near eyes | Bubble solution — always supervise, use non-toxic only
🛑 Stop and Consult
If child shows self-injury or intense meltdown during activities — pause and seek OT + SLP assessment | If child has no gaze response at all after 4 weeks — consult NeuroDev pediatrician | If significant vision concerns — ophthalmology assessment first

Disclaimer: This content is educational guidance from the Pinnacle Blooms Consortium. It does not replace evaluation by qualified SLP, OT, ABA, or NeuroDevelopmental specialists. For children with significant delays, professional assessment is essential.
📞 Not sure if it's safe to proceed? Call 9100 181 181 FREE. Our team speaks 16+ languages.
ACT II | Card 12 — Setup
The Right Space Multiplies Every Technique's Impact
🏠 Physical Space
  • Distraction-minimized room — screens off, toys put away except therapy materials
  • Child at YOUR eye level — sit on floor, kneel, use child's chair
  • You are positioned between child and the interesting materials
  • Materials held at or near your face, not at arm's length
  • Soft, warm lighting — avoid harsh fluorescents
  • Comfortable floor space for face-to-face interaction
🧠 Sensory Preparation
  • Child is regulated — not hungry, overtired, or dysregulated
  • If using light-up toys: dim room slightly for visual salience
  • Remove competing visual noise — busy backgrounds, patterned clothes
  • Volume comfortable for child — some are auditorily sensitive
⏱️ Optimal Timing
  • After morning snack (alert, regulated)
  • Mid-morning activity window (30–60 min after waking)
  • Post-afternoon nap (refreshed, receptive)
  • Avoid: immediately before/after meals, at bedtime, during dysregulation
👁️ Parent Posture Guide
  • Position your face at child's eye level
  • Use large, clear, slow pointing gestures
  • Keep your face expressively engaged — eyebrows up = interesting!
  • Leave silences — pause and WAIT for the child to look

"The best session is one that starts right. Five minutes of genuine shared attention is worth more than thirty minutes of forced interaction." — Pinnacle Protocol
ACT III — THE EXECUTION | Card 13
Before You Begin: 60-Second Readiness Assessment
Check 5 of 7 indicators before starting any joint attention session. Your child's state determines your approach — not the clock, not the schedule.
Child physically calm
No active meltdown, tantrum, or dysregulation
Child has eaten
Not hungry — food needs compete powerfully with social engagement
Child has slept adequately
Fatigue dramatically reduces social responsiveness
Familiar environment
Child is comfortable and safe in this space
No competing fixation
Child is not locked onto something that would override the activity
Caregiver is calm
Your regulated state is contagious — nervous system to nervous system
Materials are motivating
The chosen activity is genuinely interesting to THIS child today
🟢 GO (5–7 checks)
Begin the session protocol
🟡 MODIFY (3–4 checks)
Simplify — one material, shorter session, lower demand. Read cues carefully.
🔴 POSTPONE (0–2 checks)
Today is not the day. Offer calming alternative. Try at next optimal window.

"The best session is the one that starts with a child who can receive. You cannot pour connection into a dysregulated nervous system. Wait. The window will come."
ACT III | Card 14 — Step 1: Invitation
1️⃣ Step 1: Begin With an Invitation, Never a Command
"Hey, look what I have! Want to see something amazing?"

Pause. Do NOT blow yet. Hold the wand near your face. Wait 3–5 seconds. Watch for any orientation toward you.
✅ Acceptance Cues — What to Look For
  • Child looks toward you or the wand
  • Child moves their body toward you
  • Child reaches for the wand
  • Child makes any sound directed at you
Any of these = acceptance. Proceed.
Body Language Guide
  • Face open, engaged, expressive
  • Wand held just below your chin — face-adjacent height
  • Body turned fully toward child
  • No pressure — pure invitation
⚠️ Resistance Cues — What to Watch For
  • Child moves away or turns back to previous activity
  • Child begins to vocalize distress
If resistance: switch material — try the mystery box. If both refused: postpone (← Card 13 Readiness Check).

Timing: 30–60 seconds for the invitation phase. Do not rush this. The pause before the first event is where the social invitation is communicated. Your patient waiting IS the technique.
ABA Pairing Procedures | OT Just-Right Challenge | NCAEP (2020)
ACT III | Card 15 — Step 2: Engagement
2️⃣ Step 2: Deepen the Connection — Material Introduction
First Event
Child has oriented. Now: blow one small bubble. Let it float. Say "Look at that!" with genuine delight in your voice. One event. Not a stream. One.
The Pause
Wand back near your face. Look at child expectantly. Eyes wide. Eyebrows up. Say nothing. Wait. This silence is not awkward — it is the therapeutic action.
Respond to the Look
If child looks toward you (even briefly): IMMEDIATELY blow more bubbles. Timing matters — the look and the bubbles must be connected in the child's brain within 2 seconds.
Model Gaze-Following
If child's gaze tracks to the bubbles: point at a specific bubble while looking at it. "Look at THAT one!" — model gaze-following yourself. You are demonstrating the behavior you want.
Build Expectancy
After 3–4 exchanges: pause longer. 5 seconds. 7 seconds. The growing pause builds anticipation — anticipation drives social gaze toward you.
🟢 Ideal
Child looks at bubbles, then at you, then at bubbles — gaze alternation is happening
🟡 Acceptable
Child looks only at bubbles but moves body toward you when you pause
🔴 Concerning
Child shows no orientation to bubbles OR to you after 3 attempts — switch materials

Reinforcement Rule: Every time child looks toward you (even briefly) = BLOW BUBBLES. The look is the request. Honor it immediately.
PMC11506176 | ABA Reinforcement scheduling | ESDM (Early Start Denver Model) engagement principles
ACT III | Card 16 — Step 3: Therapeutic Action
3️⃣ Step 3: The Core Therapeutic Action — The Gaze Triangle
You are training the child's brain to form a gaze triangle: Child ↔ Parent ↔ Object. Every element of this step deliberately creates and reinforces this triangular gaze pattern across all 9 materials.
A — Adult-Control Pause
Control access to the interesting thing. Bubbles come from you. The toy needs you. The mystery box is yours. This positions YOU as the necessary third point of the triangle.
B — The Look-Wait
After each event, pause and look at the child with an expression of shared delight. Your face is pointing even when your finger isn't. You are modeling: "Did you see that?"
C — The Responding Moment
When the child's gaze comes toward you — OR alternates between you and the object — provide the next event within 2 seconds. You are reinforcing: "Looking toward people makes good things happen."
D — The Sharing Moment
Add declarative pointing: "Look! That one went high!" Point while looking at the object. Check if child follows the point. If yes — CELEBRATE. That is RJA. That is the technique working.
Common Execution Errors
  • ❌ Blowing bubbles continuously without pause → Fix: Always pause and wait after every burst
  • ❌ Holding wand away from face → Fix: Keep wand chin-height or temple-height
  • ❌ Talking continuously → Fix: Silence during the pause is essential
  • ❌ Moving on before child has looked → Fix: Wait. The look takes time.
  • ❌ Accepting only "perfect" eye contact → Fix: Any gaze shift toward you counts
PMC10955541 | Charman (2003) | ESDM joint attention protocols | NCAEP (2020)
ACT III | Card 17 — Step 4: Repeat & Vary
4️⃣ Step 4: 3 Great Reps Beat 10 Forced Ones
Repetition Guide
Target: 5–8 gaze-triangle moments per material per session.
Total session: 10–15 minutes across 2–3 materials.
Variation Menu — Bubbles
  • Small wand → Giant wand
  • Outdoor blowing (bubbles go higher, farther)
  • Point at specific bubbles and wait for child to follow
  • Progress: Let child hold wand — you guide to blow near face together
Variation Menu — Cause-Effect Toys
  • Change toy type each session (wind-up → pop-up → spinning)
  • Increase pause duration (2 sec → 5 sec → 8 sec before reactivating)
  • Add: Two people with toys — child must track which person to watch
Variation Menu — Books
  • Change book theme each session
  • Increase distance of point (near → slightly further)
  • Progress: "YOU point at what you want to see!"
Satiation Indicators
Stop before these appear:
  • ⚠️ Child's engagement drops (looking away, fidgeting)
  • ⚠️ Child pushes material away
  • ⚠️ Gaze quality reduces (was looking, now not)
Satiation signal = end on a SUCCESS, not a failure. Stop when child is still engaged.
The 3-Good-Reps Principle
"Three moments of genuine shared attention — eyes meeting over a shared focus — are worth more than twenty minutes of prompted, forced, mechanical 'joint attention' drills. Quality is the metric."
SI dosage literature | ESDM session structure | Pinnacle clinical protocols
ACT III | Card 18 — Step 5: Reinforce
5️⃣ Step 5: Celebrate the Attempt, Not Just the Success

The 3-Second Rule: Within 3 seconds of any joint attention behavior → deliver reinforcement. Timing matters more than magnitude. An immediate "YES! You looked!" is worth more than a delayed prize.
When child looks toward you:
"YES! You're looking at me! That's it! More bubbles!" [immediately blow]
When child follows your point:
"You saw it! You looked where I was pointing! THAT is amazing!"
When child brings something to show:
"You're showing me! You wanted ME to see! I see it! A car! I see your car!"
Type
Examples
Timing
Social praise
"Yes! Amazing! You looked!"
Immediate
Activity continuation
More bubbles, toy reactivation
Immediate
Physical celebration
High five, fist bump, clap together
Within 3 sec
Token
Sticker on chart
Within 5 sec
Preferred item
Brief access to favorite toy/food
Within 5 sec

"Even if your child looked toward you for half a second, that is a neural pathway firing. That is the social brain circuit learning to activate. Celebrate every attempt. You are building the architecture of connection, one gaze at a time."

ACT III | Card 19 — Step 6: Cool-Down
6️⃣ Step 6: End Before the Energy Does
A predictable ending is as important as a good beginning. Never abruptly stop — the child's brain needs time to close the experience gently and build positive associations with the session.
2-Minute Warning
"Two more bubbles, then all done!" Hold up two fingers. This provides predictability — the child's brain can prepare for the end without surprise or distress.
Final Shared Event
Final "event" together — last bubble, last flap, last surprise. Make this moment feel special: a little slower, a little more celebrated.
Closing Reflection
"That was so good. We looked together." Name what happened. You are building the child's understanding of what the session IS.
Transition Activity
Child participates in putting materials away (if able). Then: offer comfort item, favorite toy, or transition activity. "All done looking-together time. You did amazing."
If Child Resists Ending
  • Never abruptly remove material
  • Offer a "one more" exchange (limited to 1)
  • Introduce the transition activity as equally appealing
  • Use Canon: Transition Objects/Comfort Items
Post-Session Signs That It Worked
After a good session, children often show: increased vocal/verbal output, improved mood, reduced stimming intensity, social seeking. These are signs the social brain circuit has been activated.
NCAEP Evidence-Based Practices (2020) — Visual Supports and Transitions | Pinnacle clinical protocols

ACT III | Card 21 — Troubleshoot
When the Technique Isn't Landing: Precise Solutions
Every child is different. When something isn't working, the answer is almost never "stop trying" — it's "adjust this specific variable." Here are the most common challenges and their targeted solutions.
Problem: Child ignores bubbles completely
→ The material isn't motivating enough. Switch to highest-interest material — lights, musical toys, or mystery boxes. Joint attention requires motivation. Find the entry point that works for THIS child.
Problem: Child watches bubbles but never looks at parent
→ Move wand CLOSER to your face. Touch your chin with the wand before blowing. The gaze needs to "land" on your face on the way to the bubbles. Proximity is the key variable.
Problem: Child looks at finger, not at what you're pointing
→ Use pointing wands/puppets (Material 05). Lightly tap the target object to add movement cue. Make the endpoint more visually interesting than the finger itself.
Problem: Child takes the material and plays alone
→ Materials are NOT available independently. They only work when parent controls them. Implement briefly, without force. Try 30-second solo play, then re-engage.
Problem: Child gets frustrated when parent pauses
→ The pause is working — child is motivated! Reduce pause to 1–2 seconds initially. Accept ANY orientation (body turn, vocalization, reach) as a successful request. Build duration slowly.
Problem: Parent struggling to stay consistent
→ The most common challenge. Aim for ONE session per day rather than sporadic intensive sessions. Consistency over intensity. See community support resources.

ACT III | Card 22 — Adapt
Personalize This Technique for Your Unique Child
EASIER ← For Children Just Beginning
  • Work within arm's reach only (proximal pointing before distal)
  • Accept any body orientation toward you (not just eye gaze)
  • Use only 1 material per session
  • Sessions: 3–5 minutes maximum
  • One look = major celebration
  • Begin with person-focused games (peekaboo) before object-directed joint attention
HARDER → For Children Showing Progress
  • Increase distance of pointing targets (across the room)
  • Introduce three-person joint attention (child + 2 adults)
  • Practice IJA: "Show me your toy" — child must direct YOUR attention
  • Outdoor joint attention (more distractions = greater skill)
  • Delay reinforcement (look first, then reward after 2 complete gaze alternations)
Profile-Based Variations
For Sensory Seekers (high sensory need):
Emphasize movement-based materials — chase games, balloon play, higher energy entry. Use motor activities as the "object" of joint attention.
For Sensory Avoiders (sensory sensitive):
Quieter, calmer materials — photo books, soft puppets, mystery bags. Reduced lighting. Avoid loud instruments. Slow, predictable pace.
For Non-Verbal Children:
All techniques apply — joint attention precedes language. Accept and reinforce non-verbal sharing: reaching toward you, giving object. PECS integration possible.
For Older Children (5+ years):
Age-appropriate materials — card games, LEGOs, cooking together. Same principles: you control the interesting element, pause, wait for gaze. Academic contexts apply.
Individualized intervention planning across OT/ABA/SLP | Sensory Profile literature | ESDM adaptation protocols
ACT IV — THE PROGRESS ARC | Card 23
Weeks 1–2: The Tolerance Phase
15%
Foundation Being Laid
The social brain circuit is beginning to activate. Changes are small, real, and significant.
✅ What Progress Actually Looks Like
  • Child tolerates the session for longer each day (even 30 more seconds = progress)
  • Child's body orients slightly toward you during bubble pause
  • Child stops what they're doing when bubbles float past
  • Reduced resistance to the session (less pushing away, more staying)
  • Any vocalization directed toward you during the activity
❌ What Is NOT Progress Yet — Manage Expectations
  • Full gaze alternation (too early)
  • Child pointing back at you (too early)
  • Child "getting it" conceptually (too early)
  • Generalization to other contexts (too early)
"If your child tolerates the material for 3 seconds longer this week than last week — that is measurable neuroplasticity. That is the social brain circuit strengthening. That is real progress."

Parent Emotional Preparation: Weeks 1–2 are the hardest. The changes are tiny. The investment feels huge. This is normal. Every family navigating this journey has sat exactly where you are sitting. The arc is real. Trust the process.

ACT IV | Card 24 — Consolidation
Weeks 3–4: The Signs Most Parents Miss
40%
Neural Pathways Forming
Synaptic connections are strengthening with each successful gaze-triangle moment.
🧠 The Anticipation Signal
Child begins to orient toward the session materials BEFORE you start. They know something good is coming. This is the social brain associating YOU with positive shared experiences.
👀 Gaze Frequency Increasing
The number of looks-toward-you per session increases. Even brief, even fleeting. Track this. It is the metric that matters most in weeks 3–4.
📢 Vocal/Verbal Changes
Child may begin vocalizing during pauses — reaching, pointing, or making sounds directed at you. This is proto-requesting joint attention. Honor every instance immediately.
🎯 Gaze Length Extending
The half-second glance becomes a full-second look becomes a 2-second gaze. Duration is growing. Track the longest single gaze in each session.
🔄 First Gaze Alternations
The most exciting consolidation sign: child looks at the bubble, then at your face, then back at the bubble. This triadic gaze shift — even once — is the technique working at its deepest level.

"You may notice you are more confident too. You've found what works for your child. You've learned to read their cues. You are becoming their most effective joint attention partner. This is what parent-mediated therapy looks like."

ACT IV | Card 25 — Mastery
Weeks 5–8: Mastery Unlocked 🏆
75%
Mastery Approaching
RJA + IJA Level 1 criteria within reach. Generalization beginning.
Responding to Joint Attention (RJA) — Mastery Criteria
  • ☐ Child consistently follows parent's point to targets within reach (8/10 trials)
  • ☐ Child follows parent's gaze to near objects (without point)
  • ☐ Child resumes shared engagement after brief distraction
Initiating Joint Attention (IJA) — Mastery Criteria
  • ☐ Child brings objects to parent to show (not to request help) at least 3x per session
  • ☐ Child points at interesting things for parent to notice (proto-declarative pointing)
  • ☐ Child shows gaze alternation spontaneously: object → parent → object
Generalization Indicators
  • ☐ Skills appearing with ANOTHER communication partner (second parent, grandparent)
  • ☐ Skills appearing in a DIFFERENT setting (park, grocery store, grandparent's home)
  • ☐ Skills appearing with DIFFERENT materials (not just therapy materials)
Readiness to Progress
When child achieves 80% of mastery criteria across 3 consecutive sessions → ready for:
→ L-962: Imitation Skills Building
→ L-963: Gesture Development
→ K-801: First Words Development
PMC10955541 | BACB mastery criteria standards | NCAEP (2020)

ACT IV | Card 27 — Red Flags
5 Signals That Mean "Pause and Consult"
Trust your instincts. These specific patterns mean it's time to stop home practice and contact a professional — not because therapy isn't working, but because a different kind of support is needed first.
🚩 Zero Response to All 9 Materials Over 4 Weeks
Despite consistent, adapted attempts across all material types, child shows no orientation, no gaze shift, no interest. May indicate sensory processing barriers or regulatory issues needing OT first. Contact: Pinnacle OT + SLP assessment → 9100 181 181
🚩 Marked Regression After Initial Progress
Child was showing gains in weeks 2–3, then suddenly shows reduced engagement or new resistance. Rule out illness first. Then contact SLP/ABA teleconsult. Regression can signal environmental change or sensory overload.
🚩 Self-Injurious Behavior During Sessions
Head-banging, hitting self, biting self when joint attention is prompted. The demand level may exceed current capacity. STOP immediately. Contact ABA/BCBA for functional behavior assessment.
🚩 No Language Emergence After 8 Weeks of Mastered Joint Attention
Child achieves RJA and IJA mastery but no words or communication attempts emerge. Language should begin to "unlock" as joint attention consolidates. Speech-Language Pathology assessment urgently.
🚩 Parent Experiencing Significant Distress or Burnout
Parent feels unable to continue, overwhelmed, or hopeless. Parental wellbeing is non-negotiable. You cannot give from empty. Contact Pinnacle family support → 9100 181 181. Parent coaching available.
📞 Trust your instincts. If something feels wrong, pause and ask. 9100 181 181 | FREE | 24x7

ACT IV | Card 31 — Family Integration
Joint Attention Doesn't Stop When the Session Does
The most profound shifts in a child's development don't just happen during therapy sessions; they flourish in the 23 hours outside of them. By weaving joint attention practices into your everyday family routines, you empower your child with consistent, natural opportunities to connect and communicate.
These aren't extra tasks, but rather mindful adjustments to moments you already share, transforming ordinary interactions into powerful therapeutic experiences.
Morning Wake-Up
Point to the window, the sun, or a favorite toy as your child wakes up, waiting for their gaze to follow.
Mealtime
Name foods, point to dishes, and wait for your child's gaze to share attention when offering choices.
Bath Time
Narrate actions, use silly voices, and point to bubbles or bath toys, engaging their focus.
Outdoor Walk
Point out birds, dogs, or cars, then look back at your child to share the moment and see their reaction.
Bedtime Story
Point to pictures on the page, emphasize character expressions, and follow their gaze to what interests them.
Play Time
Follow your child's lead, join their play, and comment on what they're doing while making eye contact.

"Every shared glance across the dinner table is a therapy moment. You just have to know how to see it."
— Pinnacle Blooms SLP Team
